final_answer:
Short answer: The husband's best recourse is to file, with the immigration court that issued the August 1, 2025 in absentia order, a motion to reopen and rescind the order based on lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). That motion has no deadline and requires no filing fee. It should also request a stay of removal, which is automatic while the motion is pending. If it is granted, he can renew his adjustment of status in court, and the I-130 problem can be fixed in parallel.

1. In absentia order. Under INA 240(b)(5)(A) the court may order removal in absentia only if written notice was provided under INA 239(a). Under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), an in absentia order may be rescinded at any time on a motion to reopen showing that the alien did not receive notice in accordance with INA 239(a)(1) or (2). A notice mailed to an address the respondent never provided is not proper notice. Section 239(a)(2) change-of-address obligations attach only to an address the alien actually provided. See also 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). Because his I-130/I-485 filings listed the correct address, he should show that evidence (the filed forms, receipts, and so on). Documents the motion should include: his sworn declaration (and his wife's) that he never received the NTA, hearing notice or RFE; the I-130/I-485 as filed showing the correct address; the USCIS notices showing the wrong address; and proof he never lived at, or had any connection to, the faulty address. Many circuits require that the motion show non-receipt and a lack of fault. Courts are split on how much weight to give the presumption of delivery; the evidence should rebut it. Note the Supreme Court's Campos-Chaves v. Garland (2024) held that a defective NTA (without time and place) is cured by a later hearing notice, so each notice must be examined; here the notice was sent to a wrong address, so Campos-Chaves does not help the government. Niz-Chavez v. Garland and Pereira are also relevant to a defective NTA. A related ground, if relevant, is that the NTA was never mailed to his address of record.

2. What to file with the immigration court. A motion to reopen (no EOIR form is required, but the Immigration Court Practice Manual's formatting rules apply: cover page labelled 'Motion to Reopen - In Absentia Order', Form EOIR-33 if his address needs to be updated, proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA, and a proposed order). Attach evidence, the order of removal, and, if he is seeking relief, a copy of the application. Adjustment of status (Form I-485) with the I-130 evidence should be filed with the motion or after reopening. Because the NTA was never received, DHS may have to re-serve a proper NTA. File electronically via ECAS if possible, or by paper with the court that entered the order. File promptly: although there is no time limit for the lack-of-notice ground, delay harms credibility. Filing the motion automatically stays removal (INA 240(b)(5)(C); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)) until the IJ decides it. An appeal to the BIA lies from a denial within 30 days. A petition for review is also possible. He should also update his address by EOIR-33 and USCIS AR-11.

3. Fees. A motion to reopen filed with the immigration court ordinarily costs $145 under 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(1) plus an additional $900 (inflation-adjusted to $920 in the current year) under the 2025 H.R. 1 (OBBBA) fees. But a motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) on lack of notice is exempt: 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii) and the OBBBA exception. Therefore the fee is $0. I could not retrieve the primary text of the current fee rule, so secondary sources were relied on for the OBBBA exception. If the motion also invoked exceptional circumstances under (C)(i) (not recommended; 180-day deadline and the fee), the fee would apply. If the motion is granted and he later files Form I-485 in court, fees would apply: the I-485 filing fee is paid to DHS (not the court) with the biometrics; Form EOIR-? fees do not apply to adjustment, but he must pay the USCIS I-485 fee (currently $1,440) and the OBBBA fees may apply to certain applications in court; verify the current amounts. This was not verified.

4. The I-130 denial. Once in removal proceedings, USCIS cannot decide the I-485 (8 CFR 245.2(a)(1)); the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction to decide it (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)). A spouse's I-130 for an immediate relative can still be refiled with USCIS at any time as a new petition, and the I-130 can be pending while the IJ adjudicates. The I-130 denial for failure to respond to the RFE is an abandonment-type denial (8 CFR 103.2(b)(13)) and cannot be appealed, but a motion to reopen or reconsider on Form I-290B may be filed within 30 days (33 if mailed) of the decision (8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i), 103.8(b)). That deadline has passed; for a motion to reopen USCIS may excuse a late filing if the delay was reasonable and beyond the petitioner's control. USCIS's mailing of the RFE to a wrong address is a strong argument, but because the delay is more than two years, refiling a new I-130 (with a fee) is the safer path, and in the alternative the court can adjudicate the I-130 through USCIS. Under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15) a denial for abandonment cannot be appealed. If USCIS erred in sending the RFE to an address it should not have used, a complaint to USCIS or a mandamus/APA claim may also be explored, but with weak prospects. The spouse should file a new I-130 with the I-485 considered in court under INA 245(a) and (c); as an immediate relative who was inspected and admitted, he is not barred by 245(c) unauthorized-employment or status-violation provisions. Preconceived intent: marriage 19 days after B-2 entry invites a fraud/willful misrepresentation (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i)) inquiry, so bona fide marriage evidence and preparation are essential. This was not researched in detail.

5. Practical steps. Obtain the EOIR record (Automated Case Information 1-800-898-7180 / EOIR portal) and the FOIA file from USCIS; file the motion promptly; request a stay; update addresses; consider counsel; gather bona fide marriage evidence.

Caveat: I could not retrieve primary texts for several regulations due to access limits; verify current fee amounts and Practice Manual requirements.
